claim: The Saliva TwoStep test is based on reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP).
source: Here, we develop a simple molecular test for SARS-CoV-2 in saliva based on reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification.
evidence: The abstract directly states the test is based on RT-LAMP technology.

claim: The Saliva TwoStep test has two steps: (1) heat saliva with a stabilization solution and (2) detect virus by incubating with a primer/enzyme mix.
source: The test has two steps: (1) heat saliva with a stabilization solution and (2) detect virus by incubating with a primer/enzyme mix.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the two-step procedure of the test.

claim: Saliva samples containing the SARS-CoV-2 genome turn bright yellow after incubation in the Saliva TwoStep test.
source: After incubation, saliva samples containing the SARS-CoV-2 genome turn bright yellow.
evidence: The abstract states that positive samples turn bright yellow, which is the colorimetric readout of the test.

claim: The Saliva TwoStep test is pH dependent and can react falsely to some naturally acidic saliva samples.
source: Because this test is pH dependent, it can react falsely to some naturally acidic saliva samples.
evidence: The abstract explicitly acknowledges the pH-dependent nature of the test and potential for false positives from acidic saliva.

claim: The optimized saliva stabilization protocols rendered 295 healthy saliva samples compatible with the test, producing zero false positives.
source: We report unique saliva stabilization protocols that rendered 295 healthy saliva samples compatible with the test, producing zero false positives.
evidence: The abstract reports the specificity results from testing 295 negative samples.

claim: The Saliva TwoStep test was evaluated on 278 saliva samples from individuals who were infected with SARS-CoV-2 but had no symptoms at the time of saliva collection.
source: We also evaluated the test on 278 saliva samples from individuals who were infected with SARS-CoV-2 but had no symptoms at the time of saliva collection, and from 54 matched pairs of saliva and anterior nasal samples from infected individuals.
evidence: The abstract describes the sample cohort used for test evaluation.

claim: The Saliva TwoStep test identified infections with 94% sensitivity in individuals with sub-clinical (asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic) infections.
source: The Saliva TwoStep test described herein identified infections with 94% sensitivity and >99% specificity in individuals with sub-clinical (asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic) infections.
evidence: The abstract reports the sensitivity of the test in asymptomatic/pre-symptomatic individuals.

claim: The Saliva TwoStep test identified infections with >99% specificity in individuals with sub-clinical (asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic) infections.
source: The Saliva TwoStep test described herein identified infections with 94% sensitivity and >99% specificity in individuals with sub-clinical (asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic) infections.
evidence: The abstract reports the specificity of the test in asymptomatic/pre-symptomatic individuals.

claim: Using elevated body temperature as a sign of SARS-CoV-2 infection lacks specificity for this particular pathogen and sensitivity in identifying asymptomatic carriers.
source: However, using elevated body temperature as a sign of SARS-CoV-2 infection lacks specificity for this particular pathogen and sensitivity in identifying asymptomatic carriers (Wright and Mackowiak, 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support the claim about temperature screening limitations.

claim: LAMP (loop-mediated isothermal amplification) has existed for more than 20 years.
source: LAMP (loop-mediated isothermal amplification) is a simple nucleic acid diagnostic concept that has existed for more than 20 years (Notomi, 2000).
evidence: The introduction cites the original LAMP publication from 2000.

claim: LAMP has been used in diverse and even remote settings to test samples for the presence of viral nucleic acids.
source: It has been used in diverse and even remote settings to test samples for the presence of viral nucleic acids (Brewster et al., 2018; Chotiwan et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting the use of LAMP in various settings.

claim: LAMP utilizes loop forming primers and strand-displacement polymerases to achieve isothermal amplification of a target nucleic acid template.
source: LAMP utilizes loop forming primers and strand-displacement polymerases to achieve isothermal amplification of a target nucleic acid template, and therefore does not require a thermal cycler.
evidence: The introduction describes the basic mechanism of LAMP technology.

claim: LAMP does not require a thermal cycler.
source: LAMP utilizes loop forming primers and strand-displacement polymerases to achieve isothermal amplification of a target nucleic acid template, and therefore does not require a thermal cycler.
evidence: The introduction states that LAMP operates isothermally without a thermal cycler.

claim: LAMP assays can be performed anywhere because they simply require pipettors and a heating source as equipment.
source: LAMP assays can be performed anywhere because they simply require pipettors and a heating source (e.g. water baths or heat blocks) as equipment (Brewster et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference supporting the minimal equipment requirements for LAMP.

claim: LAMP assays offer robust amplification of target material and can produce on the order of 10^9 copies of the target in an hour-long reaction.
source: LAMP assays offer robust amplification of target material and can produce on the order of 109 copies of the target in an hour-long reaction (Notomi, 2000).
evidence: The introduction cites the original LAMP publication to support the amplification efficiency claim.

claim: Successful amplification in LAMP reactions can be directly visualized by simply looking at the reaction tube, where the reaction mix changes color upon successful target amplification.
source: Successful amplification in LAMP reactions can be directly visualized by simply looking at the reaction tube, where the reaction mix changes color upon successful target amplification.
evidence: The introduction describes the visual readout capability of LAMP assays.

claim: Colorimetric changes in LAMP can be triggered by pH indicator dyes or metal ion indicators, which change color when successful target amplification changes the chemistry within the reaction tube.
source: These colorimetric changes can be triggered by pH indicator dyes or metal ion indicators, which change color when successful target amplification changes the chemistry within the reaction tube (Kellner et al., 2020; Notomi, 2000; Tanner et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting the colorimetric detection mechanisms in LAMP.

claim: Saliva has high diagnostic value for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Recent studies have shown that saliva has high diagnostic value for SARS-CoV-2 (Butler-Laporte et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2021; Vogels et al., 2020; Wyllie et al., 2020; Yokota et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references supporting the diagnostic value of saliva for SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Compared to nasopharyngeal swabs, saliva samples harbor similar levels of viral load while being easier to obtain via self-collection.
source: Compared to nasopharyngeal swabs, saliva samples harbor similar levels of viral load while being easier to obtain via self-collection.
evidence: The introduction makes a comparative claim about saliva versus nasopharyngeal swabs.

claim: Several groups have developed RT-LAMP tests to detect SARS-CoV-2 in saliva samples.
source: Several groups have developed RT-LAMP tests to detect SARS-CoV-2 in saliva samples (Bhadra et al., 2020; Flynn et al., 2020; Lalli et al., 2020; Lamb et al., 2020; Nagura-Ikeda et al., 2020; Rabe and Cepko, 2020; Taki et al., 2021; Yokota et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references of prior RT-LAMP tests for SARS-CoV-2 in saliva.

claim: Due to pH variability between saliva samples, RT-LAMP often has a high rate of false positives when used with the common pH-dependent dye phenol red.
source: However, due to pH variability between saliva samples, RT-LAMP often has a high rate of false positives when used with the common pH-dependent dye phenol red (Bhadra et al., 2020; Hardinge and Murray, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting the false positive problem with phenol red in RT-LAMP.

claim: In RT-LAMP reactions containing phenol red, reactions start as pink/red but turn strongly yellow at pH 6.8 and below.
source: In RT-LAMP reactions containing phenol red, reactions start as pink/red but turn strongly yellow at pH 6.8 and below.
evidence: The introduction describes the pH-dependent color change of phenol red.

claim: When RT-LAMP amplifies a target, hydrogen ions are released during dNTP incorporation, causing a drop in pH within the tube to pH 6.0–6.5, triggering the color change to yellow.
source: When RT-LAMP amplifies a target, hydrogen ions are released during dNTP incorporation. This causes a drop in pH within the tube to pH 6.0–6.5, triggering the color change to yellow (Tanner et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference explaining the mechanism of pH change during LAMP amplification.

claim: Human saliva naturally varies in pH between 6.8 and 7.4.
source: Human saliva naturally varies in pH between 6.8 and 7.4 (Cameron et al., 2015), posing a significant problem in this pH-dependent assay.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for the natural pH range of human saliva.

claim: About 7% of human saliva samples are naturally acidic enough to immediately trigger phenol red-containing reactions to change to yellow without any target amplification.
source: In fact, we find about 7% of human saliva samples are naturally acidic enough to immediately trigger phenol red-containing reactions to change to yellow without any target amplification (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: The introduction references Figure 1A which shows experimental data on the prevalence of acidic saliva samples.

claim: With raw saliva, 7 of 96 tubes turned yellow before incubation, representing false positives.
source: With raw saliva, 7 of 96 tubes turned yellow at this step (highlighted in red boxes). These are false positives because no amplification reaction has occurred.
evidence: Figure 1A caption describes the false positive results observed with raw saliva.

claim: None of the 96 saliva samples mixed with saliva stabilization solution turned the reaction tube prematurely yellow.
source: None of these 96 saliva samples mixed with saliva stabilization solution turned the reaction tube prematurely yellow.
evidence: Figure 1A caption reports zero false positives when using the stabilization solution.

claim: Human saliva containing 14.5 mM NaOH is optimal to inhibit false positives caused by saliva acidity without impeding the intended color change during amplification.
source: We found that human saliva containing 14.5 mM NaOH is optimal to inhibit false positives caused by saliva acidity (N = 96; Figure 1A, right) without impeding the intended color change during amplification (Figure 1B).
evidence: The Results section describes the optimization of NaOH concentration with reference to Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The optimized saliva stabilization solution includes a chelating agent (1 mM EDTA final concentration) and Proteinase K to inhibit RNases.
source: In addition, we designed our saliva stabilization solution to also include a chelating agent (1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid [EDTA] final concentration) and Proteinase K to inhibit RNases, both of which help preserve virion RNA and therefore to increase sensitivity.
evidence: The Results section describes the components of the stabilization solution and their purposes.

claim: Proteinase K will inhibit the RT-LAMP reaction if it does not go through a heat inactivation step prior to that reaction.
source: (Note that Proteinase K will inhibit the RT-LAMP reaction if it does not go through a heat inactivation step prior to that reaction.)
evidence: The Results section notes the requirement for heat inactivation of Proteinase K.

claim: The saliva stabilization solution contains TCEP, which aids in RNA stabilization by breaking disulfide bonds present in RNases and helps to reduce saliva viscosity.
source: Finally, the saliva stabilization solution contains TCEP, which aids in RNA stabilization by breaking disulfide bonds present in RNases and helps to reduce saliva viscosity.
evidence: The Results section describes the function of TCEP in the stabilization solution.

claim: The optimized saliva stabilization solution is 2× solution: 5 mM TCEP, 2 mM EDTA, 29 mM NaOH, 100 μg/mL Proteinase K, diluted in DEPC-treated water.
source: Our optimized saliva stabilization solution (2× solution: 5 mM TCEP, 2 mM EDTA, 29 mM NaOH, 100 μg/mL Proteinase K, diluted in DEPC-treated water) is key to this test.
evidence: The Results section provides the exact composition of the stabilization solution.

claim: Heating at 95°C for 10 min degrades viral RNA when it is not in the form of virions.
source: This experiment shows that heating at 95°C for 10 min degrades viral RNA when it is not in the form of virions.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A caption describes experimental results showing RNA degradation.

claim: Heating saliva at 95°C for 10 min does not degrade viral RNA when it is in the form of virions.
source: This experiment shows that heating saliva at 95°C for 10 min does not degrades viral RNA when it is in the form of virions.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B caption describes experimental results showing RNA preservation in virions.

claim: The 'AS1E' primer set, developed by Rabe et al. and targeting the ORF1ab region of the SARS-CoV-2 genome, performs very well.
source: We found that the 'AS1E' set, developed by Rabe et al. and targeting the ORF1ab region of the SARS-CoV-2 genome, performs very well (Rabe and Cepko, 2020).
evidence: The Results section cites the source of the AS1E primer set and reports its performance.

claim: Two custom primer sets, 'ORF1e' targeting the virus ORF1ab gene and 'CU-N2' targeting the virus N gene, exhibited similar sensitivity and amplification efficiency as the AS1E set.
source: Two of our custom sets, 'ORF1e' targeting the virus ORF1ab gene and 'CU-N2' targeting the virus N gene, exhibited similar sensitivity and amplification efficiency as the AS1E set, as determined using real-time fluorescence monitoring of RT-LAMP products (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section describes the performance of custom primer sets with reference to figures.

claim: Incubation for 3 min at 95°C is sufficient to inactivate SARS-CoV-2 virions.
source: Recent studies suggest that incubation for 3 min at 95°C is sufficient to inactivate SARS-CoV-2 virions (Batéjat et al., 2021).
evidence: The Results section cites a reference supporting the heat inactivation protocol.

claim: A 10 min incubation of saliva samples at 95°C was found to be optimal for liberating viral RNA from virions.
source: A 10 min incubation of saliva samples at 95°C was found to be optimal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section references a figure showing optimization of heating time.

claim: Saliva samples containing purified virions and diluted with 2× saliva stabilization solution stored at 4°C for up to 96 hr showed no significant changes in sample stability and test detection limit.
source: We observed no significant changes in sample stability and the test detection limit over this time course, suggesting that saliva samples stored in saliva stabilization solution at 4°C are stable for at least 4 days.
evidence: The Results section describes stability testing results with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lowest concentration at which positive samples were reliably identified was 200 virions/μL in saliva.
source: The lowest concentration at which positive samples were reliably identified was 200 virions/μL in saliva (red box, summary table in Figure 3A).
evidence: The Results section reports the limit of detection with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The limit of detection refers to the virus concentration that can be identified >95% of the time.
source: Note that the limit of detection refers to the virus concentration that can be identified >95% of the time, and the assay does often detect the virus at even lower concentrations.
evidence: The Results section defines the limit of detection criterion.

claim: The ORF1e primer set was not consistent in its performance at 200 virions/μL.
source: The ORF1e primer set was not consistent in its performance at 200 virions/μL. Therefore, we decided to eliminate the ORF1e primer set from our testing panel from this point forward.
evidence: The Results section reports the decision to eliminate ORF1e based on performance data.

claim: When synthetic SARS-CoV-2 RNA is directly added to the RT-LAMP reaction mix (in the absence of saliva and the stabilization solution), the detection limit achieved was 200 genome copies/μL.
source: On the contrary, we found that when synthetic SARS-CoV-2 RNA is directly added to the RT-LAMP reaction mix (in the absence of saliva and the stabilization solution), we were unable to achieve a better detection limit than 200 genome copies/μL (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section describes control experiments with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed detection limit represents the upper performance limit of the presented RT-LAMP assay, and the saliva and stabilization solution have little to no negative impact to the test performance.
source: This suggests that the observed detection limit represents the upper performance limit of the presented RT-LAMP assay, and that the saliva and stabilization solution have little to no negative impact to the test performance.
evidence: The Results section draws an inference from the control experiment data.

claim: In a blinded study with 60 samples, only one positive sample scored as inconclusive, all negative samples were scored correctly (100% specificity), and sensitivity was 97%.
source: After running the RT-LAMP test on 60 such samples, only one positive sample scored as inconclusive. In that sample the SARS-CoV-2 primer set CU-N2 failed, while the other primer set detecting SARS-CoV-2 correctly identified the sample (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). All negative samples were scored correctly (100% specificity, binomial 95% confidence interval [88%, 100%]). Conservatively counting the inconclusive test as a false negative lead to a sensitivity estimate of 97% (binomial 95% confidence interval [93%, 100%]).
evidence: The Results section reports the blinded study results with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 screening was initiated on the University of Colorado Boulder campus starting in the summer/fall of 2020.
source: SARS-CoV-2 screening was initiated on the University of Colorado Boulder campus starting in the summer/fall of 2020.
evidence: The Results section describes the university screening program.

claim: Saliva samples were taken weekly from residents of dormitories and at several testing sites throughout the campus.
source: Saliva samples were taken weekly from residents of dormitories and at several testing sites throughout the campus.
evidence: The Results section describes the sampling protocol.

claim: Participants were asked to refrain from eating or drinking 30 min prior to sample collection, and to not participate if they were experiencing any symptoms consistent with COVID-19.
source: Participants were asked to refrain from eating or drinking 30 min prior to sample collection, and to not participate if they were experiencing any symptoms consistent with COVID-19.
evidence: The Results section describes the sample collection instructions.

claim: Individuals testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 were either pre-symptomatic at the time of saliva collection, or they never developed symptoms throughout the course of infection.
source: Therefore, individuals testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 were either pre-symptomatic at the time of saliva collection, or they never developed symptoms throughout the course of infection (we do not have the necessary follow-up data to delineate).
evidence: The Results section describes the symptomatic status of positive individuals.

claim: All saliva samples were analyzed by a quantitative RT-PCR method performed directly on saliva, which was mixed 1:1 with 2× TBE buffer containing 1% Tween-20.
source: All saliva samples were analyzed by a quantitative RT-PCR method performed directly on saliva, which was mixed 1:1 with 2× TBE buffer containing 1% Tween-20 (saliva sample prep as in Ranoa et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section describes the quantitative RT-PCR method used for comparison.

claim: An in-house multiplex quantitative RT-PCR assay was used to determine the presence of the SARS-CoV-2 genome in saliva, with primers targeting the E and N gene regions of the SARS-2-CoV genome.
source: An in-house multiplex quantitative RT-PCR assay was used to determine the presence of the SARS-CoV-2 genome in saliva, with primers targeting the E and N gene regions of the SARS-2-CoV genome (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The Results section describes the quantitative RT-PCR assay used.

claim: All positive saliva samples with viral load above the quantitative RT-PCR detection limit (N = 278), along with 295 negative saliva samples, were re-evaluated with RT-LAMP.
source: All positive saliva samples with viral load above the quantitative RT-PCR detection limit (collected between September 16–25, 2020; N = 278), along with 295 negative saliva samples, were next re-evaluated with RT-LAMP.
evidence: The Results section describes the sample set used for RT-LAMP validation.

claim: For all 573 samples, RT-LAMP with primers recognizing a human RNA positive control (RNaseP) correctly turned positive (yellow).
source: For all 573 samples, RT-LAMP with primers recognizing a human RNA positive control (RNaseP) correctly turned positive (yellow).
evidence: The Results section reports the positive control results.

claim: For all 295 SARS-CoV-2-negative samples, the AS1E and CU-N2 primer sets both returned a result of negative, consistent with the quantitative RT-PCR results.
source: For all 295 SARS-CoV-2-negative samples, the AS1E and CU-N2 primer sets both returned a result of negative, consistent with the quantitative RT-PCR results.
evidence: The Results section reports the specificity results on negative samples.

claim: There were zero false positives, and the test had a specificity of 100% in the sample set of 295 negative samples.
source: Therefore, there were zero false positives, and the test had a specificity of 100% in this extensive sample set.
evidence: The Results section reports the specificity of the test.

claim: Among all 278 positive samples, 208 (74.8%; AS1E primers) and 182 (65.5%; CU-N2 primers) returned positive RT-LAMP test results.
source: Among all positive samples, 208 (74.8%; AS1E primers) and 182 (65.5%; CU-N2 primers) returned positive RT-LAMP test results (Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section reports the sensitivity results with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: A decline in test sensitivity was observed below the experimentally determined detection limit of 200 virions/μL.
source: Although both primer sets were still able to detect SARS-CoV-2 RNA below the experimentally determined detection limit (200 virions/μL), we observed a decline in the test sensitivity below such limit (Figure 4B).
evidence: The Results section describes the relationship between viral load and sensitivity with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The observed limit of detection of the AS1E primer set was determined from human sample data to be 266 virions/µL.
source: The observed limit of detection of the AS1E primer set was determined from this data to be 266 virions/µL.
evidence: The Results section reports the limit of detection determined from human samples.

claim: Of the 168 positive samples with viral loads greater than RT-LAMP limit of detection, 158 (94%; AS1E primers) or 142 (85%; CU-N2 primers) returned positive RT-LAMP test results.
source: Of the 168 positive samples with viral loads greater than RT-LAMP limit of detection, 158 (94%; AS1E primers) or 142 (85%; CU-N2 primers) returned positive RT-LAMP test results (Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section reports the sensitivity at viral loads above the limit of detection.

claim: The differences in the observed limit of detection between the two SARS-CoV-2 primer sets could reflect the differences in the primer efficiencies, as well as the dynamics in relative viral transcript abundance.
source: The differences in the observed limit of detection between the two SARS-CoV-2 primer sets could reflect the differences in the primer efficiencies, as well as the dynamics in relative viral transcript abundance (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the primer set performance differences with a citation.

claim: Of the 278 SARS-CoV-2-positive saliva samples, 54 also had matched nasal samples collected no more than 2 days later.
source: Of the 278 SARS-CoV-2-positive saliva samples analyzed above, 54 also had matched nasal samples collected no more than 2 days later.
evidence: The Results section describes the matched sample set.

claim: Compared to the quantitative RT-PCR on saliva results, the RT-LAMP produced three false negatives in the matched sample set, whereas the Lyra nasal swab test produced eight.
source: Compared to the quantitative RT-PCR on saliva results, the RT-LAMP produced three false negatives in this sample set, whereas the Lyra nasal swab test produced eight (Figure 5A).
evidence: The Results section compares the performance of RT-LAMP to the Lyra nasal swab test with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The Saliva TwoStep test has an end-to-end processing and analysis time of approximately 45 min.
source: The two steps have an end-to-end processing and analysis time of approximately 45 min (Figure 6).
evidence: The Results section reports the total time for the test with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The use of saliva eliminates invasive nasal swab-based sampling, which requires special supplies and causes discomfort.
source: (1) The use of saliva eliminates invasive nasal swab-based sampling, which requires special supplies and causes discomfort.
evidence: The Discussion lists advantages of the saliva-based approach.

claim: The optimized saliva stabilization solution allows for analysis of a broad range of naturally acidic saliva samples while maintaining compatibility with a colorimetric RT-LAMP assay.
source: (2) We optimized a saliva stabilization solution that allows for analysis of a broad range of naturally acidic saliva samples while maintaining compatibility with a colorimetric RT-LAMP assay.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the advantages of the stabilization solution.

claim: The saliva stabilization solution helps preserve saliva samples for at least 4 days before processing and lowers saliva viscosity.
source: The solution also helps preserve saliva samples for at least 4 days before processing and lowers saliva viscosity.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the benefits of the stabilization solution.

claim: The simple heating step increases biosafety and avoids formal RNA extraction procedures.
source: (3) We determined the optimal sample heating condition that liberates the host and viral RNA with minimal degradation. The simple heating step increases biosafety and avoids formal RNA extraction procedures.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the advantages of the heating step.

claim: The AS1E and CU-N2 primers are expected to work on most or all viral variants currently circulating.
source: These primers are expected to work on most or all viral variants currently circulating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Discussion makes a claim about primer compatibility with variants with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: By strictly following the application notes, false positive results were completely avoided during the evaluation of a large cohort of human saliva samples, achieving 100% specificity.
source: By strictly following these application notes, we completely avoided false positive results during the evaluation of a large cohort of human saliva samples, achieving 100% specificity.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the specificity results.

claim: Using SARS-CoV-2-positive human saliva samples, the RT-LAMP test can consistently identify infected individuals with 94% sensitivity.
source: We also evaluated the RT-LAMP test performance based on the experimentally determined limit of detection. Using SARS-CoV-2-positive human saliva samples, we confirmed that the RT-LAMP test can consistently identify infected individuals with 94% sensitivity.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the sensitivity results.

claim: The addition of 40 mM of guanidine chloride in the RT-LAMP reaction mix did not enhance RT-LAMP amplification efficiency in the authors' experiments.
source: Previous work suggests that the addition of 40 mM of guanidine chloride in the RT-LAMP reaction mix could increase RT-LAMP amplification efficiency (Zhang et al., 2020). However, we did not observe similar enhancement when included in our experiments.
evidence: The Discussion reports negative results from testing guanidine chloride.

claim: Saliva TwoStep requires less sample processing, reaction incubation time, and laboratory overhead as compared to quantitative RT-PCR methods.
source: Saliva TwoStep requires less sample processing, reaction incubation time, and laboratory overhead as compared to quantitative RT-PCR methods.
evidence: The Discussion compares the resource requirements of Saliva TwoStep to quantitative RT-PCR.

claim: The Saliva TwoStep test can be used as a SARS-CoV-2 screening tool to reliably identify infectious individuals with minimal laboratory setup.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that the Saliva TwoStep test described herein can be used as a SARS-CoV-2 screening tool to reliably identify infectious individuals (Yang et al., 2021) with minimal laboratory setup, potentially serving as a tool for effective SARS-CoV-2 surveillance at the community level.
evidence: The Discussion concludes with the potential application of the test.

claim: With minimal set-up, the Saliva TwoStep test could be performed in diverse settings such as factories, office buildings, or schools.
source: With minimal set-up, this test could be performed in diverse settings such as factories, office buildings, or schools.
evidence: The Discussion suggests potential deployment settings for the test.

claim: Regions of the SARS-CoV-2 genome that are conserved among strains were identified using genome diversity data from NextStrain.
source: Regions of the SARS-CoV-2 genome that are conserved among strains were identified using genome diversity data from NextStrain (nextstrain.org/ncov/global).
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the primer design process.

claim: All primers should be ordered with HPLC purification, which ensures the yield and avoids cross-contamination from other SARS-CoV-2-related synthesis projects.
source: All primers should be ordered with HPLC purification, which ensures the yield and avoids cross-contamination from other SARS-CoV-2-related synthesis projects being run on the same equipment at the oligo synthesis facilities (which can lead to false positives).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides recommendations for primer ordering with a citation.

claim: The University of Colorado Boulder SARS-CoV-2 screening test was loosely based on a published quantitative RT-PCR performed directly on saliva, which has a limit of detection of 5 virions/μL.
source: The University of Colorado Boulder SARS-CoV-2 screening test was loosely based on a published quantitative RT-PCR performed directly on saliva (Ranoa et al., 2020), which has a limit of detection of 5 virions/μL.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the university testing method with a citation.
